findings.title: Async legacy writes are canceled as soon as the request context ends
findings.body: The goroutines that write to LegacyStorage (in Create at line 50-57, Delete at line 108-114, Update at line 134-141, and DeleteCollection at line 161-167) derive their timeout context from the incoming request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. The request-scoped `ctx` is canceled by the apiserver as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which for these fire-and-forget goroutines is typically before the legacy write even starts. The legacy write will then fail almost immediately with 'context canceled' (or the custom timeout cause), so mode 3 effectively never replicates writes to legacy storage in production. The timeout context must be derived from a non-cancelable context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background()), otherwise the whole point of dual-writing to legacy as a 'safe measure' is defeated.

findings.title: Legacy Update now receives raw objInfo, causing resourceVersion conflicts and store divergence
findings.body: The previous implementation wrapped the object before passing it to `d.Legacy.Update` (via `updateWrapper`), so legacy received the already-computed updated object. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to the legacy store. `objInfo.UpdatedObject` typically carries the resourceVersion/preconditions from the client request, which was read from unified storage. The legacy store has its own, different resourceVersion for the object, so the legacy update will frequently fail with a conflict (or apply a stale base object), leaving the legacy copy silently divergent from unified storage. Since legacy write errors are swallowed (only a metric bool), operators have no way to notice this drift. If raw objInfo is intentional, the conflict handling at least needs to be addressed.

findings.title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy-storage metrics
findings.body: In `Create` (line 45) and `Update` (line 129), when the write to unified Storage fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` — recording a *legacy* duration using the *storage* start time. This pollutes the legacy-write-duration metric with storage failures and makes the storage error rate invisible (the storage duration for the failed call is never recorded in these paths). The calls should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records the legacy write under the storage metric
findings.body: The async goroutine in `DeleteCollection` calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` for the legacy write. It should call `recordLegacyDuration`, as the other write methods do. As written, legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to the unified storage metric, and the legacy metric silently shows nothing, which will mislead anyone monitoring dual-write health during migration.

findings.title: Delete success path records the object name as the 'kind' metric label
findings.body: In `Delete`, the success path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object's `name` where every other call in the file passes `options.Kind`. This creates high-cardinality metric labels (one per object name) on this one code path and makes the 'kind' label inconsistent between success and failure (`options.Kind`) for the same method, breaking dashboards/alerts that aggregate by kind.

findings.title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
findings.body: In `Delete`, the enriched logger `log` (with name, kind and method values) is built at line 96, but line 97 does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` — inserting the *base* `d.Log` instead of `log`. All log statements inside Delete therefore lose the name/kind/method fields, and any logger already present in the incoming request context is replaced. Every other method in this file correctly uses `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

findings.title: Legacy write errors in the async goroutines are never logged
findings.body: In all four write paths, the error returned by the legacy store (e.g. `errObjectSt` at line 55, `err` at lines 112, 139, 165) is reduced to a boolean for the metric and then discarded — there is no `log.Error(...)` call in any of the goroutines. Because mode 3 intentionally treats legacy as a safety net, silent failures mean operators cannot distinguish 'legacy is in sync' from 'every legacy write is failing' without scraping metric internals. The error should be logged with the object name/kind so divergence can be investigated.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never assert that the async legacy write happens
findings.body: The defining new behavior of mode 3 is 'write to unified storage, then asynchronously write to legacy'. None of the mode 3 tests assert that `Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` are actually invoked after a successful storage write — there is no `m.AssertExpectations`, no wait/poll for the goroutine, and no assertion like `ls.AssertCalled(t, "Create", ...)`. The legacy mock expectations that are set up (e.g. lines 30-32, 313-315) are never verified. Additionally, because the legacy calls run in unmanaged goroutines, a testify mock may be invoked concurrently with (or after) the test body, which is a latent data race / flake. The core contract of this PR is therefore untested at the unit level.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration subtests will be flaky: legacy API is checked immediately after async legacy writes
findings.body: The new mode 3 subtests (lines 132 and 191) reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which asserts immediately after k8s writes that the legacy API returns the same data (e.g. `getFromBothAPIs` at lines 547 and 565, including `require.Equal(t, updated.GetResourceVersion(), out.GetResourceVersion())`, and the legacy list comparison at lines 523-531). In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous with no synchronization, so these assertions race the background goroutine and will intermittently fail (stale interval/title, missing item, or not-found from the legacy endpoint). These subtests need a retry/poll helper for the legacy-side checks, or the assertions must tolerate eventual consistency.
